To understand the technology of a firm, the production function is the easiest way to summarize it. General and useful ways to understand technology involve understanding firms’ production possibilities.

Measurement of Inputs and Outputs

A firm produces output from various combinations of inputs. Suppose:

  • (q)( q )(q) is the output,
  • (L)( L )(L) is labor,
  • (K)( K )(K) is capital.

We can express this relationship as:
q=f(L,K) q = f(L, K) q=f(L,K)
For specific combinations:

  • (q=f(1,2))( q = f(1, 2) )(q=f(1,2))
  • (q=f(2,2))( q = f(2, 2) )(q=f(2,2))
  • (q=f(2,1))( q = f(2, 1) )(q=f(2,1))

This representation shows the combinations of inputs and output that the firm is able to produce.

General Argument:
To study firm choices, we need a structured and convenient way to summarize the production possibilities of the firm.

Production possibilities refer to the combinations of inputs and outputs that are technologically feasible for a firm. This concept is crucial in understanding how firms utilize their resources efficiently to produce goods and services.

Key Points:

  1. Inputs and Outputs:

    • In production, both inputs (like labor and capital) and outputs (the goods produced) flow over a specific period.
    • For example, a certain amount of inputs are used to produce a specific quantity of output during that period.

  2. Time Dimension:

    • When specifying inputs, it is essential to include a time dimension.
    • For instance, labor can be measured in hours worked per week, while capital can be assessed based on the amount spent on machinery per month.
    • Important Note: It’s crucial to use the same time unit for analysis to ensure consistency.

  3. Spatial and Temporal Nature of Production:

    • Some aspects of production involve spatial and temporal considerations.
    • For example, concrete that is available in a given year may be used to construct a building in the following year.
    • Similarly, concrete used in your city might have been sourced from a neighboring state. Therefore, the input “concrete” must be understood as available in a specific location at a particular time.

Takeaway:

All these points are vital when analyzing producers’ behavior and focusing on inputs and outputs. However, it is common for us to overlook these aspects in formal discussions. This oversight does not imply that these factors are unimportant; rather, it is often assumed that they are adequately accounted for in the analysis.

The specification of technology provides a general framework that captures the same intuition but offers a different formalization for studying production behavior.

General Framework:

  • Consider a firm that has nnn possible goods.
  • This framework is general because it allows all nnn possible goods to serve as inputs and/or outputs.

Inputs and Outputs:

  • It’s easy to think of examples where certain goods act purely as inputs or outputs.
  • Examples:
    • In chemical production, heat can serve as both an input (for energy) and an output (as a byproduct).

Notation:

  • Let yjiy_j^iyji​ represent the units of good jjj used as an input.
  • Let yjoy_j^oyjo​ represent the units of good jjj produced as an output.
  • The net output of good jjj is given by:
    yj=yjo−yji y_j = y_j^o - y_j^i yj​=yjo​−yji​
  • If yjo>yjiy_j^o > y_j^iyjo​>yji​, the firm is producing more of good jjj than it is using.
  • Conversely, if yjo<yjiy_j^o < y_j^iyjo​<yji​, the firm is using more of good jjj as an input (e.g., curd) and producing less of it (e.g., heat).

Production Plan:

A production plan lists the net outputs of various goods. It can be represented as a vector:
y=(y1,y2,…,ym) y = (y_1, y_2, \ldots, y_m) y=(y1​,y2​,…,ym​)
where yyy is in Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn.

Production Possibility Set (PPS):

The set of all technologically feasible production plans is called the Production Possibility Set (PPS), denoted as YYY.

  • YYY is obviously a subset of Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn and describes all patterns of inputs and outputs that are technologically feasible, providing a complete description of the firm’s technological possibilities.

Examining Technological Possibility Set:

We may want to distinguish between production plans that are “immediately” feasible and those that are “eventually” feasible. This distinction aligns with the familiar discussion of the short run (SR) and the long run (LR).

Short Run vs. Long Run:

  • In the short run, since some factors are fixed, production plans must take these restrictions into account.
  • We will assume that all restrictions faced by the firm in the short run are described by a vector zzz in Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn.
    • Think of zzz as the list of the maximum amounts of various inputs and outputs that can be produced in the concerned period.

Restricted Production Possibility Set:

We use a restricted production possibility set denoted by Y(z)Y(z)Y(z) (in the short run, this is called the SR PPS).
Y(z)={y∈Y:Yj=yj} Y(z) = \{ y \in Y : Y_j = y_j \} Y(z)={y∈Y:Yj​=yj​}

  • Here, Y(z)Y(z)Y(z) consists of all feasible net output bundles consistent with the set of restrictions.
  • Example: If a factor is fixed at yny_nyn​ in the SR, then the SR PPS can be defined as:
    Y(yˉn)={y∈Y:yn=yˉn} Y(\bar y_n ) = \{ y \in Y : y_n =\bar y_n \} Y(yˉ​n​)={y∈Y:yn​=yˉ​n​}

Conclusion:

The set Y(z)Y(z)Y(z) is a subset of YYY because it contains all production plans that satisfy the additional conditions imposed by the input requirements.

Suppose a firm produces a single output, denoted as yyy, while the rest of the goods are inputs. We can denote the vector of inputs as x=(x1,x2,…,xn)x = (x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n)x=(x1​,x2​,…,xn​). The production process can be expressed as the net output bundle (y,−x)(y, - x)(y,−x), where yyy represents the units of output produced.

A special case of the restricted production possibilities set is the input requirement set, denoted as V(y)V(y)V(y). It is defined as:
V(y)={x∈R+n:(y,−x)∈Y} V(y) = \{ x \in \mathbb{R}^n_+ : (y, -x) \in Y \} V(y)={x∈R+n​:(y,−x)∈Y}
This set describes the real space of nnn dimensions in the positive space.

Properties of V(y)V(y)V(y):

  • V(y)V(y)V(y) has two parts:
    1. All inputs are constrained in the positive real space.
    2. The net output bundle associated with these inputs is technologically feasible.

Thus, V(y)V(y)V(y) is the set of all input bundles that can produce at least yyy units of output.

Important Note:

The input requirement set defines inputs as positive numbers, which is the opposite of how inputs are defined in the Production Possibility Set (PPS).

Isoquant Definition

We can define an isoquant using the concept of the input requirement set. Let V(y)V(y)V(y) be the set of all input bundles producing at least yyy units of output.

For all input bundles that produce exactly yyy units of output, we define:
Q(y)={x∈R+n:x∈V(y) and x produces exactly y units of output} Q(y) = \{ x \in \mathbb{R}^n_+ : x \in V(y) \text{ and } x \text{ produces exactly } y \text{ units of output} \} Q(y)={x∈R+n​:x∈V(y) and x produces exactly y units of output}

Example: Short Run Production Possibility Set (SR PPS)

Suppose a firm produces output from labor and capital. The production plan can be represented as (y,−l,−k)(y, -l, -k)(y,−l,−k), leading to the PPS defined as:
Y={(y,−l,−k)∈Y} Y = \{ (y, -l, -k) \in Y \} Y={(y,−l,−k)∈Y}

Now, if we can change the labor input but the capital is fixed at kˉ\bar kkˉ, then we have:
Y(z)→Y(kˉ)={(y,−l,−k)∈Y:k=kˉ} Y(z) \rightarrow Y(\bar k) = \{ (y, -l, -k) \in Y : k = \bar k \} Y(z)→Y(kˉ)={(y,−l,−k)∈Y:k=kˉ}
This shows how the production possibility set adjusts based on fixed and variable inputs in the short run.

Production Function

If a firm produces one output, we define the production function as follows:
f(x)={y∈R:y is the maximum output associated with x in Y} f(x) = \{ y \in \mathbb{R} : y \text{ is the maximum output associated with } x \text{ in } Y \} f(x)={y∈R:y is the maximum output associated with x in Y}
This function relates the input vector xxx to the maximum possible output yyy that can be produced by the firm.

Transformation Function

The concept of a production function can be extended into a higher dimensional analog, known as the transformation function. It is defined as:
T:Rn→R T : \mathbb{R}^n \rightarrow \mathbb{R} T:Rn→R
The transformation function T(y)=0T(y) = 0T(y)=0 if and only if yyy represents an efficient production plan.

What do we mean by “efficient”?

A production plan yyy is said to be efficient if there is no other production plan y′y'y′ such that y≤y′y \leq y'y≤y′ and y′≠yy' \neq yy′=y. In simple terms, this means that a production plan is efficient if there is no way to produce more output with the same inputs or produce the same output with fewer inputs.

Summary:

We have explored the key technical and formal methods used to describe various aspects of production possibilities. We will now focus on the description of the methods used. In this part of the course, we focus on the assumption that a firm is producing a single output, and much of the analysis revolves around describing the technology using the input requirement set V(y)V(y)V(y) and the transformation function T(y)T(y)T(y).

This focuses on how to describe production processes. The simplest way to describe production using input requirement sets is to simply list them!

Example:

Suppose we have an output good, produced using two factor inputs: factor 1 and factor 2. There are two different activities or techniques by which this production takes place. To produce 1 unit of the output good, we can do either of the following:

  1. Technique 1: 1 unit of factor 1 and 2 units of factor 2 →\rightarrow→ 1 unit of output.
  2. Technique 2: 2 units of factor 1 and 1 unit of factor 2 →\rightarrow→ 1 unit of output.

Now, let’s further define the goods:

  • Suppose output is good 1.
  • Input 1 is good 2.
  • Input 2 is good 3.

Production Possibility Set:

Y={(1,−2,−1),(1,−1,−2)} Y = \{(1, -2, -1), (1, -1, -2)\} Y={(1,−2,−1),(1,−1,−2)}

Input Requirement Set:

For 1 unit of output, the input requirement set is:
V(1)={(2,1),(1,2)} V(1) = \{(2, 1), (1, 2)\} V(1)={(2,1),(1,2)}

Now, if I ask you, what is V(y)V(y)V(y)? That is, what is the set of feasible ways to produce yyy units of output?

V(y)={(y,2y),(2y,y)} V(y) = \{(y, 2y), (2y, y)\} V(y)={(y,2y),(2y,y)}

Does this set include all relevant possibilities? Not quite! Why?

  • It is true that (y,2y)(y, 2y)(y,2y) produces yyy units if we use technique A.
  • Similarly, (2y,y)(2y, y)(2y,y) produces yyy units if we use technique B.

But what if we use a mixture of techniques A and B?

Accurate Input Requirement Set:

Let us try to formulate a more accurate input requirement set for y=1,2,…y = 1, 2, \dotsy=1,2,…. Let:

  • YAY_AYA​ be the amount of output produced by technique A.
  • YBY_BYB​ be the amount of output produced by technique B.

The input requirement set for yyy can then be written as:
V(y)={(YA+2YB,YB+2YA):y=YA+YB} V(y) = \{(Y_A + 2Y_B, Y_B + 2Y_A): y = Y_A + Y_B \} V(y)={(YA​+2YB​,YB​+2YA​):y=YA​+YB​}

So, for example:

  • V(1)={(1,2),(2,1)}V(1) = \{(1, 2), (2, 1)\}V(1)={(1,2),(2,1)}
  • V(2)={(2,4),(4,2),(3,3)}V(2) = \{(2, 4), (4, 2), (3, 3)\}V(2)={(2,4),(4,2),(3,3)}
  • V(3)={(3,6),(6,3),(5,4),(4,5)}V(3) = \{(3, 6), (6, 3), (5, 4), (4, 5)\}V(3)={(3,6),(6,3),(5,4),(4,5)}

And so on…

Thus, for the given technological specification, the set:
V(y)={(YA+2YB,2YA+YB):y=YA+YB} V(y) = \{(Y_A + 2Y_B, 2Y_A + Y_B): y = Y_A + Y_B \} V(y)={(YA​+2YB​,2YA​+YB​):y=YA​+YB​}
is a more appropriate description of the input requirement set.

The concept of Returns to Scale (RTS) refers to how the output of a production process changes when all inputs are scaled up or down by the same proportion. There are three main types of returns to scale:

1. Constant Returns to Scale (CRS):

A technology exhibits Constant Returns to Scale (CRS) if, when all inputs are multiplied by a scalar factor ttt, the output is also multiplied by ttt. Mathematically, a production function (f(x1,x2,…,xn))(f(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n) )(f(x1​,x2​,…,xn​)) exhibits CRS if either of the following conditions is satisfied:

  1. f(tx)=tf(x)f(tx) = t f(x)f(tx)=tf(x) for all t>0t > 0t>0, where xxx represents the vector of input quantities.
  2. The production function is homogeneous of degree 1, meaning that scaling inputs by a factor ttt scales the output by the same factor.

But is CRS always a reasonable assumption?

  • Not always. It may be possible to scale up production processes, but scaling down is often not trivial. Scaling down could result in hitting the minimum scale of production, beyond which further reduction may not be economically viable.

    • For example, scaling up by integer multiples is possible, but scaling down may hit a limit, where production becomes inefficient.

  • Also, while scaling up, it’s possible to encounter increasing efficiencies in certain production processes. For example, doubling all inputs might lead to more than double the output.

Example: Oil Pipeline

Consider a firm building an oil pipeline between two points, say A and B. If we double all inputs (such as materials, labor, etc.), the output (oil transported) might more than double. This happens because:

  • The surface area of the pipeline increases by a factor of 2.
  • But the volume of oil transported increases by a factor of 4, indicating Increasing Returns to Scale (IRS).

2. Increasing Returns to Scale (IRS):

A production function exhibits Increasing Returns to Scale (IRS) if, when all inputs are multiplied by a scalar t>1t > 1t>1, the output increases by more than ttt. Mathematically:
f(tx)>tf(x)for allt>1 f(tx) > t f(x) \quad \text{for all} \quad t > 1 f(tx)>tf(x)for allt>1

Example: The pipeline scenario discussed above is an example of IRS, where doubling the inputs leads to more than double the output.

Another way CRS might be violated is when certain inputs cannot be replicated, like agricultural land or specific natural resources, leading to IRS.

3. Decreasing Returns to Scale (DRS):

A production function exhibits Decreasing Returns to Scale (DRS) if, when all inputs are multiplied by a scalar t>1t > 1t>1, the output increases by less than ttt. Mathematically:
f(tx)<tf(x)for allt>1 f(tx) < t f(x) \quad \text{for all} \quad t > 1 f(tx)<tf(x)for allt>1

DRS typically arises when certain inputs are not easily replicable, such as specialized labor or land, leading to restricted production possibilities.

A function f(x)f(x)f(x) is homogeneous of degree kkk if:

f(tx)=tk⋅f(x)for all t>0 f(tx) = t^k \cdot f(x) \quad \text{for all} \, t > 0 f(tx)=tk⋅f(x)for allt>0

This property describes how a production function responds to proportional changes in all inputs. There are two important special cases of homogeneity:

  • Homogeneous of degree 0:
    f(tx)=f(x) f(tx) = f(x) f(tx)=f(x)
    This indicates that the output remains unchanged when all inputs are scaled by a factor ttt.

  • Homogeneous of degree 1:
    f(tx)=t⋅f(x) f(tx) = t \cdot f(x) f(tx)=t⋅f(x)

A homothetic function is defined as a monotonic transformation of a function that is homogeneous of degree 1.

This means the output f(x)f(x)f(x) is a transformed version of a homogeneous function of degree 1.

Why Study Homogeneous and Homothetic Functions?

  1. Homogeneous Functions:

    • Many well-behaved production functions in economics are homogeneous of degree 1, which is directly related to CRS technology.
    • Homogeneous functions of degree 1 imply that output scales proportionally with inputs, which is a crucial assumption in many economic models.

  2. Homothetic Functions:

    • Homothetic functions allow for flexibility because they include a monotonic transformation of a CRS technology.
    • These transformations enable us to measure output in different units (e.g., converting kilograms to pounds) without altering the fundamental relationship between inputs and outputs.

For instance, changing from kilograms to pounds is a simple monotonic transformation. However, if we apply a more complex transformation, such as squaring or taking the square root of the output, the output may change non-linearly.

In the figures, we can describe the behavior of isoquants for homogeneous and homothetic functions as follows:

  • Homogeneous Isoquants:

    • Hence, homogeneous isoquants represent a situation where scaling up all inputs by the same factor leads to an exact doubling of output.

  • Homothetic Isoquants:

    • Homothetic isoquants, therefore, show that output has increased, but the magnitude of the increase is ambiguous and depends on the specific monotonic transformation applied.

What is Profit?

In economics, profit is defined as the difference between the revenue a firm receives and the costs it incurs during the production of goods and services.

We have already learned that economic cost is different from the cost as defined in accountancy. In accountancy, cost represents anything the business has explicitly paid for, and we can calculate accounting costs by simply examining the company’s balance sheet. However, economic costs represent a “what if” scenario for your business. These costs include both explicit costs (like those in accountancy) and implicit costs.

Implicit costs refer to those costs that are not recorded in the ledger but represent the opportunity cost of using resources. For instance, if a person owns a business, they forego the salary they could have earned working elsewhere. This foregone salary is considered an implicit cost of running the current business.

Now, both the revenue and costs of a firm depend on the decisions or actions taken by the firm. These actions can include production activities, purchasing inputs, advertising expenses, innovation efforts, etc.

Suppose we write these actions as a1,a2,…,ana_1, a_2, \ldots, a_na1​,a2​,…,an​.

This condition suggests that profit is maximized when the marginal revenue (MR) from an additional unit of aia_iai​ equals the marginal cost (MC). The intuition behind this is:

This fundamental condition can be applied in several ways:

  • The firm can decide the quantity of output to produce using this condition.
  • The firm can also determine the amount of labor to hire based on this condition.

The second fundamental condition is the condition of long-run profits. If two firms have identical revenue and cost functions, then in the long run, they cannot have equal profits. Why? Because the firm earning lower profit can imitate the actions of the other firm and claim the same amount of profit.

How do we get these functions from the profit maximization solution?

These functions are derived from the profit maximization problem, which implies certain restrictions on the behavior of the demand and supply functions.

If we multiply all of the prices by some positive number ttt, the vector of factor input that maximizes profit π\piπ will not change.

Proof:

The profit function is defined as:

π=P⋅f(x)−w⋅x \pi = P \cdot f(x) - w \cdot x π=P⋅f(x)−w⋅x

where PPP is the output price, f(x)f(x)f(x) is the production function, www is the input price, and xxx is the quantity of input.

The first-order condition (F.O.C.) for profit maximization is given by:

Now, consider multiplying all prices by a positive scalar ttt:

The F.O.C. remains the same:

xi(tP,tw)=xi(P,w) x_i(tP, tw) = x_i(P, w) xi​(tP,tw)=xi​(P,w)

This proves that factor demand functions are homogeneous of degree zero.

Implications:

This property is important because it provides a way to verify if an observed production plan is generated by a firm maximizing profits. Specifically, factor demand functions should be homogeneous of degree zero.

Practical Uses of This Property:

  1. Theoretical Examination:

    • We can use this property to make theoretical statements about how a profit-maximizing firm would respond to changes in its economic environment (e.g., changes in prices).

  2. Empirical Validation:

    • We can empirically test if a firm’s observed demand functions exhibit patterns consistent with profit maximization. For example, if prices double but the firm’s demand and supplies change, the firm is not a profit maximizer.

Example:

If a firm’s demand and supplies change when prices double without any other change, the firm is not a profit maximizer. This contradicts the property that demand functions should be homogeneous of degree zero.

There are three main methods:

  1. First-order conditions (F.O.C.):

  2. Direct Examination of the Demand and Supply Functions:

    • By examining the maximizing properties of demand and supply functions directly.

  3. Properties of the Profit and Cost Functions:

    • By analyzing how profit and cost functions respond to changes in prices and other factors.

Comparative static analysis involves examining how optimal choices respond to changes in the economic environment. In particular, we are interested in the sensitivity of optimal choices to changes in one of the parameters of the model.

Comparative static analysis helps us understand how a firm’s optimal decisions (e.g., input choices, output levels) change in response to exogenous shocks to the model, such as changes in prices or technology.

content:
The profit function contains all the economically relevant information about the firm’s behavior. We can use the profit function to derive the firm’s net supply functions.

Suppose we have the firm’s supply function y(p)y(p)y(p). And we want the profit function - what do we do? This is easy. We substitute this into our profit expression and get π(p)=p⋅y(p)\pi(p) = p \cdot y(p)π(p)=p⋅y(p).

Now, suppose we have the profit function and are asked to find the firm’s supply function - How?

We use the Hotelling’s Lemma:

Let yi(p)y_i(p)yi​(p) be the firm’s net supply function of good iii. Then:

yi(p)=∂π(p)∂piy_i(p) = \frac{\partial \pi(p)}{\partial p_i}yi​(p)=∂pi​∂π(p)​ for i=1,...,ni = 1, ..., ni=1,...,n

assuming that this derivative exists and pi>0p_i > 0pi​>0.

Proof:

Suppose y∗y^*y∗ is a profit-maximizing net output vector at prices p∗p^*p∗. Then we define a function:

g(p)=π(p)−p⋅y∗g(p) = \pi(p) - p \cdot y^*g(p)=π(p)−p⋅y∗

Here π(p)=p⋅y\pi(p) = p \cdot yπ(p)=p⋅y is the profit function. Thus, the profit-maximizing plan at price ppp will be at least as good as y∗y^*y∗, since y∗y^*y∗ is feasible but not necessarily optimal at prices ppp.

This implies that g(p)≥0g(p) \ge 0g(p)≥0 for all ppp and g(p∗)=0g(p^*) = 0g(p∗)=0. Therefore, g(p)g(p)g(p) attains a minimum at p=p∗p = p^*p=p∗.

Assuming that π(p)\pi(p)π(p) is differentiable, the first-order condition for a minimum is:

∇g(p∗)=0\nabla g(p^*) = 0∇g(p∗)=0

This gives us:

∂π(p∗)∂pi−yi∗=0\frac{\partial \pi(p^*)}{\partial p_i} - y_i^* = 0∂pi​∂π(p∗)​−yi∗​=0

or

yi∗=∂π(p∗)∂piy_i^* = \frac{\partial \pi(p^*)}{\partial p_i}yi∗​=∂pi​∂π(p∗)​

Since this holds for any price vector p∗p^*p∗, we have:

yi(p)=∂π(p)∂piy_i(p) = \frac{\partial \pi(p)}{\partial p_i}yi​(p)=∂pi​∂π(p)​

This completes the proof.

Intuitive Explanation:

Hotelling’s Lemma states that the firm’s net supply function for a good is equal to the partial derivative of the profit function with respect to the price of that good. Intuitively, this means that a small increase in the price of a good will lead to an increase in the firm’s supply of that good, proportional to the derivative of the profit function.

Implications:

Hotelling’s Lemma is a powerful tool for analyzing firm behavior. It allows us to:

  • Derive the firm’s supply function directly from its profit function.
  • Analyze how changes in prices affect the firm’s supply decisions.
  • Understand the relationship between the firm’s profit-maximizing behavior and its supply function.

Note:

The assumption of differentiability of the profit function is crucial for Hotelling’s Lemma to hold. If the profit function is not differentiable, the supply function may not be well-defined.

Let us consider a single output and a single input case.

The profit function of a firm can be expressed as:

Π(x)=P⋅f(x)−w⋅x\Pi(x) = P \cdot f(x) - w \cdot xΠ(x)=P⋅f(x)−w⋅x

where:

  • PPP is the price of the output.
  • f(x)f(x)f(x) is the production function, representing the output produced using input xxx.
  • www is the price of the input.

The first-order condition (F.O.C) for profit maximization is:

P⋅df(x)dx−w=0P \cdot \frac{df(x)}{dx} - w = 0P⋅dxdf(x)​−w=0

This condition gives us the demand function for the input, x(P,w)x(P,w)x(P,w), which represents the optimal amount of input demanded by the firm at given prices PPP and www.

Substituting the demand function back into the profit function, we get:

Π(P,w)=P⋅f(x(P,w))−w⋅x(P,w)\Pi(P,w) = P \cdot f(x(P,w)) - w \cdot x(P,w)Π(P,w)=P⋅f(x(P,w))−w⋅x(P,w)

This is the profit function expressed in terms of the prices of output and input.

Differentiating the profit function with respect to www, we get:

∂π∂w=P⋅∂f(x(P,w))∂x⋅∂x∂w−w⋅∂x∂w−x(P,w)\frac{\partial \pi}{\partial w} = P \cdot \frac{\partial f(x(P,w))}{\partial x} \cdot \frac{\partial x}{\partial w} - w \cdot \frac{\partial x}{\partial w} - x(P,w)∂w∂π​=P⋅∂x∂f(x(P,w))​⋅∂w∂x​−w⋅∂w∂x​−x(P,w)

Rearranging and using the F.O.C, we get:

∂π∂w=[P⋅∂f(x(P,w))∂x−w]⋅∂x∂w−x(P,w)=−x(P,w)\frac{\partial \pi}{\partial w} = [P \cdot \frac{\partial f(x(P,w))}{\partial x} - w] \cdot \frac{\partial x}{\partial w} - x(P,w) = -x(P,w)∂w∂π​=[P⋅∂x∂f(x(P,w))​−w]⋅∂w∂x​−x(P,w)=−x(P,w)

This result demonstrates the economic rationale behind Hotelling’s lemma, which states that the derivative of the profit function with respect to the input price is equal to the negative of the input demand function.

Economic Rationale:

When the price of an output increases, there are two effects:

  1. Direct effect: The price increase leads to higher profits even at the same level of output. This is because the revenue increases while the cost remains the same.
  2. Indirect effect: The increase in price induces the firm to change its level of output by a small amount. This is because the firm wants to take advantage of the higher price by producing more output. However, since the input is already at its profit-maximizing level, the indirect effect will be zero.

This is an application of the Envelope Theorem, which states that the derivative of the maximized value of a function with respect to a parameter is equal to the derivative of the objective function with respect to the parameter, holding the choice variables constant at their optimal values.

The Envelope Theorem

Consider a maximization problem with parameter aaa:

M(a)=max⁡xf(x,a)M(a) = \max_x f(x,a)M(a)=maxx​f(x,a)

M(a)M(a)M(a) is the maximized value of the function, which is a function of the parameter aaa.

Let x(a)x(a)x(a) be the value of xxx that solves the problem. Then:

M(a)=f(x(a),a)M(a) = f(x(a),a)M(a)=f(x(a),a)

This simply says that the optimized value of the function is equal to the function evaluated at the optimal choice of xxx.

Differentiating both sides with respect to aaa, we get:

dM(a)da=∂f(x(a),a)∂x⋅dx(a)da+∂f(x(a),a)∂a\frac{dM(a)}{da} = \frac{\partial f(x(a),a)}{\partial x} \cdot \frac{dx(a)}{da} + \frac{\partial f(x(a),a)}{\partial a}dadM(a)​=∂x∂f(x(a),a)​⋅dadx(a)​+∂a∂f(x(a),a)​

The first term on the right-hand side represents the indirect effect of aaa on M(a)M(a)M(a) through the change in the optimal choice of xxx. The second term represents the direct effect of aaa on M(a)M(a)M(a), holding xxx constant at its optimal value.

The Envelope Theorem states that the indirect effect is zero, i.e.,

∂f(x(a),a)∂x⋅dx(a)da=0\frac{\partial f(x(a),a)}{\partial x} \cdot \frac{dx(a)}{da} = 0∂x∂f(x(a),a)​⋅dadx(a)​=0

This is because at the optimal choice of xxx, the derivative of the objective function with respect to xxx is zero.

Therefore, we have:

dM(a)da=∂f(x(a),a)∂a\frac{dM(a)}{da} = \frac{\partial f(x(a),a)}{\partial a}dadM(a)​=∂a∂f(x(a),a)​

This means that the derivative of the maximized value of the function with respect to a parameter is equal to the derivative of the objective function with respect to the parameter, holding the choice variables constant at their optimal values.

Applying Hotelling’s Lemma to a Simple One-Input, One-Output Profit Maximization

Consider a firm that uses a single input, xxx, to produce a single output, yyy. The firm’s production function is y=f(x)y = f(x)y=f(x), and the prices of the output and input are ppp and www, respectively.

The firm’s profit function is:

π(p,w)=max⁡x[p⋅f(x)−w⋅x]\pi(p,w) = \max_x [p \cdot f(x) - w \cdot x]π(p,w)=maxx​[p⋅f(x)−w⋅x]

The first-order condition for profit maximization is:

p⋅f′(x)−w=0p \cdot f'(x) - w = 0p⋅f′(x)−w=0

This condition implicitly defines the firm’s demand function for the input, x(p,w)x(p,w)x(p,w).

Applying Hotelling’s Lemma, we can find the firm’s supply function for the output:

y(p,w)=∂π(p,w)∂p=f(x(p,w))y(p,w) = \frac{\partial \pi(p,w)}{\partial p} = f(x(p,w))y(p,w)=∂p∂π(p,w)​=f(x(p,w))

This result is intuitive: the firm’s supply of output is simply the output produced using the optimal amount of input.

Similarly, we can find the firm’s demand function for the input:

x(p,w)=−∂π(p,w)∂w=x(p,w)x(p,w) = -\frac{\partial \pi(p,w)}{\partial w} = x(p,w)x(p,w)=−∂w∂π(p,w)​=x(p,w)

∂y(p,w)∂p=f′(x(p,w))⋅∂x(p,w)∂p\frac{\partial y(p,w)}{\partial p} = f'(x(p,w)) \cdot \frac{\partial x(p,w)}{\partial p}∂p∂y(p,w)​=f′(x(p,w))⋅∂p∂x(p,w)​

The first term on the right-hand side, f′(x(p,w))f'(x(p,w))f′(x(p,w)), is the marginal product of the input. The second term, ∂x(p,w)∂p\frac{\partial x(p,w)}{\partial p}∂p∂x(p,w)​, is the derivative of the input demand function with respect to the output price.

The right-hand side is the second derivative of the profit function with respect to the input price. In the short run (SR), the average cost behaves differently due to its two components: fixed costs and variable costs.

  • Short-run average fixed cost (SAFC) decreases as output increases, as fixed costs are spread over more units.

  • Short-run average variable cost (SAVC) is typically U-shaped due to the principle of variable proportions:

    1. Increasing Returns: Initially, as more of the variable factor is used, the SAVC falls because less input is required for each additional unit of output.

    2. Constant Returns: At some level of output, the SAVC remains constant.

    3. Decreasing Returns: Eventually, as more of the variable factor is added, the SAVC rises due to diminishing marginal returns.

Combining SAFC and SAVC results in the overall average cost (AC). Initially, AC decreases because of the decreasing SAFC and SAVC. However, after a certain point, the increasing SAVC causes the overall AC to rise.

The output level at which average cost is minimized is referred to as the minimal efficient scale.

In the long run (LR), all costs are variable. Therefore, the phenomenon of increasing average costs seems unreasonable since a firm can replicate its production process efficiently without facing the constraints present in the short run.

In conclusion, understanding the geometry of costs helps firms determine the optimal level of production and pricing strategies while considering both fixed and variable factors.

Relationship Between LR and SR Cost Curves

The LR cost curve can never be above any SR cost curve because, in the LR, even fixed factors can be adjusted. This leads to unconstrained optimization, which results in better outcomes.

The LR cost function can be expressed as:

c(y)=c(y,z(y)) c(y) = c(y, z(y)) c(y)=c(y,z(y))

Thus, the LR and SR cost curves must be tangent at the point y∗y^*y∗.

Therefore, if the total cost curves in the SR and the LR are tangent to each other, the LR and SR average cost (AC) curves must also be tangent.

Family of Short-Run Average Cost (SRAC) Curves

Consider a family of SRAC curves corresponding to a fixed factor zzz. Let zzz take three possible values: z1z_1z1​, z2z_2z2​, and z3z_3z3​. The associated SRACs are denoted as SAC1SAC_1SAC1​, SAC2SAC_2SAC2​, and SAC3SAC_3SAC3​.

The LR average cost (LAC) for this family of SAC curves is the lower envelope of these SR cost curves. This is because the optimal choice of zzz to produce yyy is the choice that minimizes the cost of producing yyy.

Consequently, the LAC curve will have a scallop shape, representing the lower envelope of the SRAC curves.

Examining the Concavity Property in Detail

Similar to the proof of the convexity of the profit function, we can graph cost as a function of the price of a single input while holding all other prices constant.

If the price of this factor rises, it implies that costs will not decrease (as stated in property 1), but they will increase at a decreasing rate. This occurs because, as the factor becomes more expensive, firms will substitute it with cheaper inputs.

Basic Intuition Behind the Proposition

When we operate at a cost-minimizing point and the price w1w_1w1​ increases, there are both direct and indirect effects to consider:

  • Direct Effect: The expenditure on the first factor will increase.

  • Indirect Effect: We may substitute to cheaper inputs, causing a change in the factor mix. However, since we are operating at a cost-minimizing point, any infinitesimal change must yield zero additional profit.

  1. Non-Decreasing in Factor Prices:
    The cost function is non-decreasing in factor prices, expressed as:

We have previously derived the cost function for various specifications of technology by solving the cost-minimizing problem.

However, this process can be reversed: given a cost function, we can solve for a technology that conveys essentially the same information as the production function.

Any concept defined in terms of the properties of the production function has a ‘dual’ definition in terms of the properties of the cost function, and vice versa. This relationship embodies the principle of ‘duality’.

Application of Duality

Suppose we have the cost function:

c=(w1+w2)y. c = (w_1 + w_2)y. c=(w1​+w2​)y.

To find the underlying production function, we can use Shephard’s lemma, which states:

∂c∂w1=x1and∂c∂w2=x2. \frac{\partial c}{\partial w_1} = x_1 \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{\partial c}{\partial w_2} = x_2. ∂w1​∂c​=x1​and∂w2​∂c​=x2​.

From the cost function, we also have:

∂c∂w1=∂c∂w2=y. \frac{\partial c}{\partial w_1} = \frac{\partial c}{\partial w_2} = y. ∂w1​∂c​=∂w2​∂c​=y.

This implies:

x1=x2=y. x_1 = x_2 = y. x1​=x2​=y.

Thus, the production function can be expressed as:

y=min⁡(x1,x2). y = \min(x_1, x_2). y=min(x1​,x2​).

Geometry of Duality

The geometry of duality illustrates the relationship between a firm’s technology, summarized by its production function, and its economic behavior, represented by its cost function.

Isocost Line

An isocost line represents different combinations of factor prices that yield the same level of cost. In a two-good framework, we can express the isocost line as:

dw2dw1=−∂c∂w1∂c∂w2=−x1x2(from Shephard’s lemma) \frac{dw_2}{dw_1} = \frac{-\frac{\partial c}{\partial w_1}}{\frac{\partial c}{\partial w_2}} = \frac{-x_1}{x_2} \quad \text{(from Shephard's lemma)} dw1​dw2​​=∂w2​∂c​−∂w1​∂c​​=x2​−x1​​(from Shephard’s lemma)

Slope of an Isoquant

The slope of an isoquant can be defined as:

dx2dx1=−∂f∂x1∂f∂x2=−w1∗w2∗(at the F.O.C) \frac{dx_2}{dx_1} = \frac{-\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}}{\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}} = \frac{-w_1^*}{w_2^*} \quad \text{(at the F.O.C)} dx1​dx2​​=∂x2​∂f​−∂x1​∂f​​=w2∗​−w1∗​​(at the F.O.C)

This highlights a key duality property:

  1. The slope of the isoquant is the ratio of factor prices.
  2. The slope of the isocost curve is the ratio of factor levels.

Curvature Relationship

The curvatures of the isocost curve and isoquant are inversely related:

  • If the isocost curve is very curved, the isoquant will be relatively flat, and vice versa.

Movement on the Isocost Curve

Consider any point (w1,w2)(w_1, w_2)(w1​,w2​) on the isocost curve. If we move to another point (w1′,w2′)(w_1', w_2')(w1′​,w2′​) on the same isocost curve, and suppose the slope doesn’t change much (indicating less curvature), then the ratio of factor demands will correspond to the slope. Consequently, the cost-minimizing bundles must be similar, leading to curved isoquants that tend toward a Leontief production function.

This relationship between isocost and isoquant curves illustrates the principles of duality in economic theory.

Consider a smooth, convex isoquant. In this case, the isocost curve is also convex, which implies that demand curves are well-behaved.

Flat Spot on Isoquant

If the isoquant has a flat spot, this indicates that factor prices for that portion yield the same factor demands. Consequently, the isocost curve becomes non-differentiable at that point, resulting in conditional factor demand functions that are multivalued.

Kink on Isoquant

Suppose the isoquant has a kink at some point. For a certain range of prices, a fixed bundle of inputs is demanded, leading to a flat spot on the isocost curve.

Non-Convex Isoquant

If the isoquant is non-convex over some range, the isocost curve will exhibit a kink, resulting in conditional factor demand curves that are both discontinuous and multivalued.

Conclusion

In these scenarios, the demand curve becomes indistinguishable from the previous cases, highlighting the complex relationship between production functions, cost functions, and conditional factor demands.

Uses of Duality

Duality has several important consequences:

  1. Convenience in Description: Having two different ways to describe technological properties is theoretically convenient. We can utilize either a cost function or a profit function instead of relying solely on the direct technology.

  2. Importance in Equilibrium Analysis: Dual representation is crucial and useful in equilibrium analysis. It allows us to discuss the behavior of the firm without needing to solve for explicit equilibrium solutions.

Up until now, we have studied the maximizing behavior of individual firms. Now, we will focus on how market prices are determined by the actions of individual agents.

Single Competitive Market

Competitive Firm:

A competitive firm is one that accepts the market price of output as given and beyond its control. In a competitive market, each firm perceives the price as independent of its own actions, although the collective actions of all firms together determine the market price.

Let π\piπ be the market price. The demand curve facing an ideal competitive firm takes the form:

D(π)→Firm Demand Curve D(\pi) \rightarrow \text{Firm Demand Curve} D(π)→Firm Demand Curve

  • A competitive firm cannot set any price it desires or produce any quantity it wants.

However, why is this the case?

  1. If the price is above the market price, it implies zero demand.
  2. If the price is below the market price, the firm can sell as much as it wants, but it will forgo potential profits.
  3. If the price equals the market price, the firm can sell as much as it wants, as profit-seeking behavior will push the price as high as possible.

Thus, a competitive firm faces an infinitely elastic demand curve.

Examples of Competitive Markets in the Real World:

  • Genuine goods such as fruits and cement.

In this section, we investigate the welfare properties of a competitive equilibrium using the representative consumer approach.

Representative Consumer Model

Let the market demand curve x(p)x(p)x(p) be generated by maximizing the utility of a single representative consumer. The consumer has a quasilinear utility function given by:

u(x)+y u(x) + y u(x)+y

Here:

  • xxx represents the good we focus on.
  • yyy represents everything else, which can be thought of as the money left over after the consumer makes optimal expenditures on the good xxx.

Properties of Quasilinear Utility Function

A quasilinear utility function has the following key properties:

  1. The demand curve is independent of money income.
  2. The demand curve is unaffected by the prices of other goods.

Utility Maximization

To maximize utility U(x,y)U(x, y)U(x,y), subject to the budget constraint, we have:

max⁡U(x,y)=U(x)+ys.t.M=Px⋅x+y \max U(x, y) = U(x) + y \quad \text{s.t.} \quad M = P_x \cdot x + y maxU(x,y)=U(x)+ys.t.M=Px​⋅x+y

From this, we can express yyy in terms of the budget constraint:

U(x,y)=U(x)+M−Px⋅x  ⟹  y=M−Px⋅x U(x, y) = U(x) + M - P_x \cdot x \quad \implies \quad y = M - P_x \cdot x U(x,y)=U(x)+M−Px​⋅x⟹y=M−Px​⋅x

Taking the derivative of the utility function, we find:

U′(x,y)=U′(x)−Px=0 U'(x, y) = U'(x) - P_x = 0 U′(x,y)=U′(x)−Px​=0

This leads us to the condition:

U′(x)=Px U'(x) = P_x U′(x)=Px​

or, equivalently:

P=u′(x) P = u'(x) P=u′(x)

The inverse of this function represents the supply function:

u′(x(p))=p u'(x(p)) = p u′(x(p))=p

Representative Firm Model

Alongside the representative consumer, we also assume a representative firm with a cost function c(x)c(x)c(x).

We interpret this cost function such that the production of xxx units of output requires c(x)c(x)c(x) units of the good yyy.

The equilibrium profit-maximizing condition thus yields:

p=c′(x) p = c'(x) p=c′(x)

This condition indicates the level of output at which the marginal willingness to pay equals the marginal cost of production.

Now, suppose that instead of using the market mechanism to determine xxx, we directly determine the amount of output that maximizes the consumer’s utility.

Utility Maximization Problem

We want to maximize:

max⁡u(x)+ys.t.y=w−c(x) \max u(x) + y \quad \text{s.t.} \quad y = w - c(x) maxu(x)+ys.t.y=w−c(x)

Here, www is the endowment of the yyy-good. Thus, we can rewrite the objective as:

max⁡u(x)+w−c(x) \max u(x) + w - c(x) maxu(x)+w−c(x)

First-Order Condition

Taking the first-order condition (F.O.C.), we have:

u′(x)−c′(x)=0 u'(x) - c'(x) = 0 u′(x)−c′(x)=0

This simplifies to:

u′(x)=c′(x) u'(x) = c'(x) u′(x)=c′(x)

Thus, the competitive market result in production is exactly the same level of production and consumption as that obtained by maximizing utility directly.

Welfare Maximization Problem

The welfare maximization problem can be formulated as maximizing total utility:

W=u(x)+h(consuming y-good) W = u(x) + h \quad \text{(consuming } y\text{-good)} W=u(x)+h(consuming y-good)

Since consuming xxx units of the xxx-good means giving up c(x)c(x)c(x) units of the yyy-good, the social objective can be expressed as:

Social Objective=u(x)+w−c(x) \text{Social Objective} = u(x) + w - c(x) Social Objective=u(x)+w−c(x)

This leads to the formulation:

Arg max u(x)+w−c(x)=Arg max (u(x)−c(x))(15) \text{Arg max } u(x) + w - c(x) = \text{Arg max } (u(x) - c(x)) \quad \text{(15)} Arg max u(x)+w−c(x)=Arg max (u(x)−c(x))(15)

Economic Interpretation

What is u(x)u(x)u(x)? It represents the area under the inverse demand curve up to xxx.

Similarly, c(x)c(x)c(x) represents the area under the marginal cost (MC) curve up to xxx.

Hence, choosing xxx to maximize utility minus costs is equivalent to maximizing the area between the demand and supply curves.

Alternate Approach

Using consumer surplus and producer surplus, we can express:

  • Consumer Surplus:

cs(x)=u(x)−Px⋅x cs(x) = u(x) - P_x \cdot x cs(x)=u(x)−Px​⋅x

  • Producer Surplus:

ps(x)=Px⋅x−c(x) ps(x) = P_x \cdot x - c(x) ps(x)=Px​⋅x−c(x)

The social welfare can then be expressed as:

SW=cs(x)+ps(x) SW = cs(x) + ps(x) SW=cs(x)+ps(x)

This simplifies to:

SW=u(x)−Px⋅x+Px⋅x−c(x)=u(x)−c(x) SW = u(x) - P_x \cdot x + P_x \cdot x - c(x) = u(x) - c(x) SW=u(x)−Px​⋅x+Px​⋅x−c(x)=u(x)−c(x)

Thus, we conclude that the competitive equilibrium maximizes total surplus.

A Pareto efficient allocation is one for which there is no way to make all agents better off; to make one agent better off, the other must be worse off.

Thus, a Pareto efficient allocation is one that maximizes the utility of agent 1 while holding agent 2 fixed at some given level of utility.

Maximize u1(x1)+y1 \text{Maximize } u_1(x_1) + y_1 Maximize u1​(x1​)+y1​
subject to
u2(x‾−x1)+(y‾−y1)=u‾2 u_2(\overline{x} - x_1) + (\overline{y} - y_1) = \overline{u}_2 u2​(x−x1​)+(y​−y1​)=u2​

This can be rewritten as:

Maximize u1(x1)+u2(x‾−x1)+y‾−u‾2 \text{Maximize } u_1(x_1) + u_2(\overline{x} - x_1) + \overline{y} - \overline{u}_2 Maximize u1​(x1​)+u2​(x−x1​)+y​−u2​

First-Order Conditions

Taking the first-order conditions gives us:

u1′(x1)=u2′(x‾−x1) u_1'(x_1) = u_2'(\overline{x} - x_1) u1′​(x1​)=u2′​(x−x1​)

For any given value of x1x_1x1​, this condition will uniquely determine an efficient level of x2=x‾−x1x_2 = \overline{x} - x_1x2​=x−x1​.

Arbitrary Distribution of yyy

The distribution of y1y_1y1​ and y2y_2y2​ is arbitrary. Transferring the yyy-good back and forth between agents 1 and 2 makes one agent better off and the other worse off, but does not affect the marginal conditions for efficiency at all.

Competitive Equilibrium

How does the condition u1′(x1)=u2′(x2)u_1'(x_1) = u_2'(x_2)u1′​(x1​)=u2′​(x2​) fare as a competitive equilibrium?

At equilibrium, we have:

u1′(x1)=u2′(x‾−x1)=P∗ u_1'(x_1) = u_2'(\overline{x} - x_1) = P^* u1′​(x1​)=u2′​(x−x1​)=P∗

Hence, the necessary condition for Pareto efficiency is satisfied. Furthermore, any allocation that is Pareto efficient must satisfy this condition.

content:
How can we obtain the same result when we maximize the sum of welfare and when we solve the Pareto efficient problem? Let’s delve deeper into this.

Two Consumers and Two Goods

We consider two consumers and two goods, with the initial amounts as follows:

  • Good xxx: x‾\overline{x}x
  • Good yyy: y‾\overline{y}y​

Efficient Allocation

The efficient allocation can be expressed as:

Maximize u1(x1)+y1 \text{Maximize } u_1(x_1) + y_1 Maximize u1​(x1​)+y1​

subject to

u2(x‾−x1)+(y‾−y1)=u‾2 u_2(\overline{x} - x_1) + (\overline{y} - y_1) = \overline{u}_2 u2​(x−x1​)+(y​−y1​)=u2​

Sum of Utilities

The sum of utilities maximization problem can be written as:

Maximize u1(x1)+u2(x‾−x1)+y1+(y‾−y1) \text{Maximize } u_1(x_1) + u_2(\overline{x} - x_1) + y_1 + (\overline{y} - y_1) Maximize u1​(x1​)+u2​(x−x1​)+y1​+(y​−y1​)

Conclusion

We know that the same optimal value x∗x^*x∗ will solve both problems! However, the allocation of the yyy-good that satisfies these conditions is different. Any pair (y1,y2)(y_1, y_2)(y1​,y2​) can maximize the sum of utilities, but there will be only one specific value of y1y_1y1​ that satisfies the efficient allocation condition.

Thus, the efficient allocation solution is just one of the many solutions that can arise from maximizing the sum of utilities.

The utility achieved by a consumer with income mmm facing a price ppp when she purchases good xxx is given by:

u(0,m) u(0, m) u(0,m)

Using quasilinear preferences, we have:

u(1)+m−r=u(0)+m u(1) + m - r = u(0) + m u(1)+m−r=u(0)+m

r=u(1)−u(0) r = u(1) - u(0) r=u(1)−u(0)

Since u(0)=0u(0) = 0u(0)=0, it simplifies to:

r=u(1) r = u(1) r=u(1)

Thus, by consuming good xxx, the consumer achieves a utility level of:

u(1)+m−p at price P=r+m−p u(1) + m - p \text{ at price } P = r + m - p u(1)+m−p at price P=r+m−p

Effect of a Tax

  • Demand Price: PdP_dPd​
  • Supply Price: PsP_sPs​

A quantity tax is imposed on the amount of the good consumed, leading to the relationship:

Pd=Ps+t P_d = P_s + t Pd​=Ps​+t

A value tax is a percentage tax on the expenditure of a good, represented as:

Sg⋅Pd=(1+e)⋅Ps S_g \cdot P_d = (1 + e) \cdot P_s Sg​⋅Pd​=(1+e)⋅Ps​

Demand and Supply Functions

Demand depends on the demand price PdP_dPd​, denoted as D(Pd)D(P_d)D(Pd​), and similarly, the supply function is S(Ps)S(P_s)S(Ps​).

The equilibrium condition can be expressed as:

D(Pd)=S(Ps) D(P_d) = S(P_s) D(Pd​)=S(Ps​)

With the tax relationship:

Pd=Ps+t P_d = P_s + t Pd​=Ps​+t

Substituting gives:

D(Ps+t)=S(Ps) D(P_s + t) = S(P_s) D(Ps​+t)=S(Ps​)

Which can also be rearranged to:

D(Pd)=S(Pd−t) D(P_d) = S(P_d - t) D(Pd​)=S(Pd​−t)

Inverse Demand and Supply Functions

Alternatively, the relationships can be expressed using the inverse demand and supply functions:

Pd(x)=Ps(x)+t P_d(x) = P_s(x) + t Pd​(x)=Ps​(x)+t

or

Ps(y)=Pd(y)−t P_s(y) = P_d(y) - t Ps​(y)=Pd​(y)−t

Welfare Analysis

  • Consumer Surplus (CS):

CS=u(xd)−Pd⋅xd CS = u(x^d) - P_d \cdot x^d CS=u(xd)−Pd​⋅xd

  • Producer Surplus (PS):

PS=Ps⋅xs−c(xs) PS = P_s \cdot x^s - c(x^s) PS=Ps​⋅xs−c(xs)

  • Tax Revenue (T_ax):

Tax=(Pd−Ps)⋅x∗ T_{ax} = (P_d - P_s) \cdot x^* Tax​=(Pd​−Ps​)⋅x∗
